solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Guy’s husband wearing baseball attire

indicators.note: what you wear goes around you, so one item sits inside the garment

blocks.note: a baseball cap is the standard headgear of the sport
H is the standard abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: A man's husband is dressed up in baseball kit.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'is', joining definition to wordplay rather than marking possession.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are informal British terms for a man or fellow, so they are straightforward synonyms.

clue.text: They run fast and they play dirty, we’re told

indicators.note: being told something means hearing it spoken, so the sound matters rather than the spelling

blocks.note: people who play dirty are cheaters, said in a non-rhotic British accent

explanation.surface: A sports team accused of being both quick and foul.
explanation.walkthrough: In standard British speech the final R of cheaters is silent, so it sounds just like the big cats.
explanation.definitionFit: The big spotted cats are famous as the fastest land animals, so runners at speed describes them.

clue.text: Wow, a puzzle that has dead ends?

blocks.note: taken as written
a labyrinth of paths, many of which lead nowhere

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims at a labyrinth, wondering whether it has dead ends.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wow' looks like an exclamation but is used as a verb here; 'that has dead ends' just describes the puzzle, with 'dead ends' completing its picture.
explanation.definitionFit: To wow an audience is to astonish or impress them greatly, a verb synonym.

clue.text: Corn periodically safe to eat and easy to swallow?

indicators.note: something done periodically happens at regular intervals, so only every other letter is kept

blocks.note: first and third letters of the word
edible food is safe to eat

explanation.surface: Is this corn safe and easy to get down?
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that 'easy to swallow' is meant figuratively, as in believing a story, not digesting food.
explanation.definitionFit: A story people readily swallow is one they find believable, so the idiom means plausible.

clue.text: Once again cut grass with it

blocks.note: a reed is a tall grass of wet ground
taken as written

explanation.surface: Instructions to mow the lawn a second time using some tool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut' suggests mowing, but here it is editorial cutting of a text or film.
explanation.definitionFit: Editors cut material, so cutting a manuscript or film a second time is editing it anew.

clue.text: Maybe shift round to get seats offering a good view?

blocks.note: a shift is a type of simple dress; 'maybe' marks it as an example
a round is a circle

explanation.surface: Perhaps move round to find seats with a better view.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shift' reads as a verb meaning move, but it is the loose straight dress. The dress circle is the first raised tier of seats in a theatre.
explanation.definitionFit: The theatre's first balcony tier looks down over the stage, so those places give spectators a fine outlook.

clue.text: Surround bees flying around island, say

indicators.note: things flying about are scattered, so the letters are thrown into a new order
to be around something is to enclose it on both sides

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
I is the standard abbreviation for island
e.g. means for example, as does say

explanation.surface: A swarm of bees circling an island.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged bees wrap around both the island letter and the abbreviation for 'for example'.
explanation.definitionFit: An army besieging a town surrounds it to cut it off, so the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Female from Reading regularly heading for Andover

indicators.note: doing something regularly means at fixed intervals, so every other letter is taken
the heading of something is its top or front, so only the opening letter counts

blocks.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters
the opening letter of the town

explanation.surface: A woman from Reading often travels to Andover.
explanation.walkthrough: Reading and Andover are both English towns, which makes 'heading for' read as travel. A girl's name clued as 'Female' is a common crossword liberty.
explanation.definitionFit: Edna is a woman's given name, so any woman so called is an example of a female.

clue.text: Specimen is no longer enough

blocks.note: an ex is something that is no longer what it was, as in ex-wife
ample means enough or more than enough

explanation.surface: A sample that once sufficed no longer does.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is' links the definition to the two-part wordplay rather than belonging to the sentence's meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: A specimen is one item taken to show what the whole class is like, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Two or three prepare anaesthetic

definitions.note: the definition gives two examples; the answer names one of them

blocks.note: to prime a surface or pump is to prepare it
something that numbs, read as numb-er

explanation.surface: A doctor readying a couple of doses of anaesthetic.
explanation.walkthrough: NUMBER must be read as 'numb-er', a thing that numbs, not the counting word; 'Two or three' sounds like a quantity of doses.
explanation.definitionFit: Both two and three are divisible only by one and themselves, so either is an instance of this mathematical class.

clue.text: European head travelling west somewhere in Germany

indicators.note: in an across clue west is leftward, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: E is the standard abbreviation for European
a ness is a headland, as in Loch Ness's neighbour Ness points

explanation.surface: A European leader heading west to a German destination.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head' is a promontory here, as is ness, the word found in place names like Sheerness.
explanation.definitionFit: Essen is an industrial city in the Ruhr, so it is a place located inside Germany.

clue.text: Huge site is renovated to house British street paper

indicators.note: renovating a building reworks it, so the letters are rebuilt in another order
a house holds its occupants, so one part is placed inside the other

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
B is the standard abbreviation for British

explanation.surface: A giant site being refurbished to accommodate a British newspaper office.
explanation.walkthrough: The Big Issue is a British magazine sold on the street by homeless vendors, who keep part of the price.
explanation.definitionFit: The magazine is sold by vendors on pavements, so it is literally a publication traded in the street.

clue.text: Don’t change that boy’s hats

blocks.note: stet is the proofreader's instruction to let a deletion stand
son's, belonging to the boy

explanation.surface: Telling someone to leave a boy's hats alone.
explanation.walkthrough: Stet is Latin for 'let it stand', written in a margin to cancel a correction.
explanation.definitionFit: A Stetson is the wide-brimmed cowboy hat, named after its maker, so these are kinds of headwear.

clue.text: Fly from Athens, possibly

indicators.note: possibly suggests one of several arrangements, so the letters may take another form

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Catching a plane out of the Greek capital, perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fly' reads as air travel, but here it means rush.
explanation.definitionFit: To fly is to move quickly or hurry, as in 'I must fly', which matches the verb.

clue.text: Extremely snobbish sanction having little depth

indicators.note: the extremes of something are its two ends, so only the outermost letters remain

blocks.note: first and last letters
to sanction is to permit or allow

explanation.surface: A very snobbish person approving of something superficial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely' looks like an intensifier for snobbish but picks out its two ends.
explanation.definitionFit: Shallow water or thought lacks depth, so the adjective and the phrase match directly.

clue.text: Be in control of bad credit

indicators.note: something bad is spoiled or wrong, so the letters are put out of order

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Managing someone's poor credit rating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bad credit' reads as a financial phrase, but 'bad' only signals rearranging the second word.
explanation.definitionFit: To direct a film or business is to manage and run it, a verb synonym for control.

clue.text: Small creatures found in silver mines

indicators.note: something found in a place lies within it, so the letters sit inside the words that follow

blocks.note: runs across the two words

explanation.surface: Little animals living in old silver mines.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer straddles the gap between the two final words, starting partway into the metal.
explanation.definitionFit: Vermin are rats, mice and similar pests, typically small animals regarded as nuisances.

clue.text: Mark’s clever, in a manner of speaking

blocks.note: an acute mind is sharp and clever
an accent is a regional way of pronouncing words

explanation.surface: Someone called Mark is, so to speak, a clever fellow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mark' poses as a man's name but is a written sign; the 's is 'is'. 'In' links the two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The acute accent is a diacritic, the small sloping stroke written over a letter as in café.

clue.text: Thoroughly enjoy each place when climbing

indicators.note: in a down clue climbing means reading upward, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: EA is the standard abbreviation for each
to place something is to put it

explanation.surface: Loving every spot when out climbing.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the second piece turns around; the abbreviation stays as it is.
explanation.definitionFit: To eat something up, figuratively, is to relish it eagerly, as an audience eats up praise.

clue.text: Mary Somerville, for one, appears in first couple of science books

indicators.note: the first couple of anything is its opening pair, so only two leading letters are taken

blocks.note: the opening two letters
OT is the Old Testament, the first books of the Bible

explanation.surface: A famous woman scientist features in the opening pages of science books.
explanation.walkthrough: Mary Somerville was a nineteenth-century Scottish mathematician and science writer, so she fits the surface's science books too.
explanation.definitionFit: Somerville was born in Jedburgh and raised in Scotland, so she is one example of a person from that nation.

clue.text: In France, LeBron is a big star

indicators.note: what is in something is held inside it, so the letters lie within the words that follow

blocks.note: runs across the two words, ignoring the comma

explanation.surface: The basketball star LeBron James is famous even in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In France' looks like a setting, but 'In' is the hiding signal and the country's name supplies the first letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A celeb, short for celebrity, is a famous person, which is what a big star is.

clue.text: Expert teams deployed (or recalled)

indicators.note: deploying troops spreads them into new positions, so the letters are rearranged
something recalled is called back, so the letters go backwards

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
taken as written

explanation.surface: Specialist squads are sent out, or perhaps brought back home.
explanation.walkthrough: The brackets make 'or recalled' look like an aside, but it is a piece of wordplay in its own right.
explanation.definitionFit: A maestro is a master of an art, originally a great conductor, so a virtuoso or skilled authority.

clue.text: Very tall wife breaks piece of foot jewellery

indicators.note: breaking into something means forcing a way inside it, so one part ends up enclosed

blocks.note: a toe ring is jewellery worn on the foot
W is the standard abbreviation for wife

explanation.surface: A tall woman snaps her husband's gift of an anklet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very tall wife' reads as one phrase, but the definition stops at 'tall'.
explanation.definitionFit: Towering describes something rising to a great height, like a skyscraper, so it means extremely high.

clue.text: Phone purchases are priced pretty stupidly to begin with

indicators.note: what comes to begin with is at the start, so only each word's opening letter counts

blocks.note: the opening letter of each of the four words

explanation.surface: A complaint that mobile phone downloads cost a silly amount.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a grumble about pricing; the first letters of its four words spell the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Apps are software applications bought from a store and installed on a smartphone.
